findings.premise: Switching withWriteTxn, the migration runner and the first-boot write from root.transaction to root.childTransaction makes a throwing callback's writes abort while the caller still gets its own error. This covers every part of the ISSUE's fix intent: all three sites, the original error, the bounded lock-loss wait, tests after a reopen, and the corrected migration comment.
findings.evidence: Outside a write txn, childTransaction calls `this.transactionAsync(callback, true)` (node_modules/lmdb/write.js:939). In executeTxnCallbacks, the asChild branch runs `env.beginTxn(1); // abortable` and on a catch runs `env.abortTxn(); txnError(error, txnCallbacks, j)` (write.js:663-680). It also awaits a thenable result before it commits (:669-671), so the migration runner's async step and its version write are aborted together when the step rejects. The caller's promise rethrows `txnCallbacks.errors[txnIndex]` (:966-969). ISSUE.md:23 asks for all three sites, the original error, the lock-loss handling, tests after a reopen and the comment fix. LLD §2.1-2.3, §4 and Migration step 1 cover each of them. [files: node_modules/lmdb/write.js, docs/standalone/graph-store-write-transaction-whose-callback-E202610165437d6e5/ISSUE.md]

findings.premise: Today root.transaction commits a throwing callback's writes: the plain-callback branch records the error and does not abort the shared batch txn. withWriteTxn (store.ts:886), the migration runner (migrations.ts:442-448) and the first-boot write (store.ts:607-610) all use it.
findings.evidence: `transaction(callback)` delegates to `this.transactionAsync(callback)` (write.js:897-902). Its plain branch is `try { let result = userTxnCallback(); ... } catch (error) { txnError(error, txnCallbacks, j); }` (write.js:683-692), and nothing in that branch calls abortTxn. store.ts:886: `store.root.transaction(() => fn(store))`. migrations.ts:442: `await store.root.transaction(async () => { await step.run(store); ... await store.meta.put(META_SCHEMA_VERSION, step.to); })`. store.ts:607: `await root.transaction(() => { writeSchemaVersion(...); provisionSharedModulesRows(store); })`. [files: node_modules/lmdb/write.js, src/db/graph/store.ts, src/db/graph/migrations.ts]

findings.premise: Production code has only three root.transaction call sites, and all 52 production withWriteTxn callers pass synchronous callbacks. The narrowed synchronous-only type therefore breaks only the one async test callback (store-health.test.ts:152).
findings.evidence: Grep of `.transaction(` under src finds production code only at store.ts:607, store.ts:886 and migrations.ts:442. Every other hit is a test or test helper (lmdb-smoke, store-child, migration-v2-to-v3, derived-indices). Grep of withWriteTxn calls outside __tests__ gives config/store 3, todos 11, relations 10, doc-summaries 3, repos 3, ids 3, entities 4, conversations 13 and exploration-cache 2, which is 52 calls. Each one is a plain `s => {...}` or `s => fn(s)` arrow. Grep for `withWriteTxn(async` finds only src/db/graph/__tests__/store-health.test.ts:152. [files: src/db/graph/store.ts, src/db/graph/migrations.ts, src/db/graph/__tests__/store-health.test.ts]

findings.premise: The bounded wait and lost-lock reporting in withWriteTxn stay unchanged. childTransaction, called outside a write txn, returns the same queued promise shape as transaction, so the race, confirmLockLoss and recordLocksLost('a write transaction','write-timeout-probe') keep working. The store is opened without useWritemap, so childTransaction does not throw.
findings.evidence: childTransaction: `if (useWritemap) throw ...; if (writeTxn) {...nested...} return this.transactionAsync(callback, true);` (write.js:904-939). This is the same transactionAsync promise that transaction returns (:902), so it rejects with the stored error (:966-969) or never settles. store.ts:888-908 races that promise against the probe timer and needs no change. store.ts:523-527 calls `open({ path, mapSize, maxDbs })` and passes no useWritemap. [files: src/db/graph/store.ts, node_modules/lmdb/write.js]

findings.premise: Migration steps can stay async inside one child transaction because they run inside getGraphStore's open, before any caller can obtain the store. After locks-lost, no library transaction (now including childTransaction) is called.
findings.evidence: getGraphStore returns `_instance` only after it is set at store.ts:641 (`_instance = store;`). That comes after the migration call at :621, and concurrent callers await `_initPromise` (:501), so no withWriteTxn can queue during a step. After locks-lost, getGraphStore throws at :499 before any transaction call, and withWriteTxn awaits getGraphStore first (:885). store-health.test.ts:84-107 counts the patched transaction and transactionSync calls. The LLD extends that count to childTransaction. [files: src/db/graph/store.ts, src/db/graph/__tests__/store-health.test.ts]

findings.premise: Each acceptance criterion has a test that would fail without the fix. ac1 and ac2 read the rows back (in-process and after a reopen) with a stated mutation check. The current migration test asserts only the version, so the row assertions are new and would fail on root.transaction.
findings.evidence: migrations.test.ts:151-176 asserts the rejection (:159), `ranA` (:164), the version (:165, :175) and `applied` (:174). It never checks rows, so the LLD's added row assertions are what expose the defect. Without the fix, a row written before a throw survives (write.js:683-692), so write-txn-atomic.test.ts and the extended migration test would fail on the current code. ac3 is a preservation criterion: lock-loss-detection.test.ts is meant to stay unchanged, and the store-health childTransaction count is new. ac4 pins the library's keep/discard behaviour (write.js:683-692 vs :663-680 vs :1024-1027), so an lmdb upgrade that changes it would fail the test. [files: src/db/graph/__tests__/migrations.test.ts, node_modules/lmdb/write.js]

summary.prose: Every write transaction of the graph store becomes all-or-nothing when its callback throws. The store's write helper, the schema migration runner and the first-boot write switch from lmdb's batched transaction, which commits a failed callback's writes, to its child transaction, which aborts them, while keeping the batching and the bounded wait for a store that lost its locks. Tests pin the library behaviour and read the results back after reopening the store.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Standalone feature — no parent HLD. Design directly against the repo, grounded on the s1 analyze passes. There are no HLD shared contracts to honour.

boundary.internal: LLD for ISSUE-5437d6e5: make every graph-store write transaction all-or-nothing when its callback throws (withWriteTxn, the migration runner, the first-boot write), keeping withWriteTxn bounded lock-loss handling, with regression tests read back in the same process and after a reopen.

api.name: withWriteTxn
api.signature: function withWriteTxn<T>(fn: (store: GraphStore) => T extends PromiseLike<unknown> ? never : T): Promise<T>  // src/db/graph/store.ts:882; the callback must be synchronous

parameters.name: fn
parameters.type: (store: GraphStore) => T (synchronous; a Promise-returning callback is a compile-time error)

returns.meaning: The callback's result once its writes are committed.

errors.condition: The callback threw: the promise rejects with that same error and none of the callback's writes are kept.
The store lost its locks (as today: the bounded wait's probe, or confirmLockLoss on a thrown write error).
The callback returned a thenable: the child transaction is aborted and the promise rejects with 'withWriteTxn callbacks must be synchronous' (nothing is kept).

postconditions: The callback must be synchronous: an async child callback keeps lmdb's write transaction open across its await, and a second caller arriving then would run nested inside it and lose its writes if the first throws (probed), so a thenable result is refused and aborted.

The callback runs as an lmdb child transaction (`store.root.childTransaction(() => fn(store))` in place of `store.root.transaction(...)` at :886): if it throws, every write it made is aborted, while other callers' writes queued in the same batch are committed.

On success the writes commit exactly as today, in lmdb's shared batch; the promise keeps its async shape, so the race against the probe timer, confirmLockLoss and recordLocksLost('a write transaction', 'write-timeout-probe', ...) are unchanged.

withWriteTxn wraps the library's result in Promise.resolve, so a value returned by a nested child transaction (lmdb's `when` returns a plain value there) cannot break the `.then` chain at src/db/graph/store.ts:886.

api.name: runMigrations
api.signature: function runMigrations(store: GraphStore, stored: number, target: number, registry?: readonly Migration[]): Promise<number>  // src/db/graph/migrations.ts; signature unchanged

errors.condition: A step threw: the run rejects with it, and neither that step's writes nor its version write are kept; earlier steps stay committed.

postconditions: Each step and its version write run in one `store.root.childTransaction(async () => { ... })`, so a throwing step leaves the store exactly as it was before that step.
The comment at :444-446 says what holds: a thrown step aborts its own writes and the version write.
Steps may stay async: migrations run inside getGraphStore's open, before any caller can obtain the store, so no other writer can interleave with a step's child transaction.

api.name: getGraphStore
api.signature: function getGraphStore(): Promise<GraphStore>  // src/db/graph/store.ts; signature unchanged
postconditions: The first-boot write (src/db/graph/store.ts:607-610: the schema version and the shared-modules rows) runs in `root.childTransaction`, so a throw there leaves no partial first boot.

api.name: withWriteTxnSync
api.signature: function withWriteTxnSync<T>(store: GraphStore, fn: () => T): T  // src/db/graph/store.ts:935; unchanged
postconditions: Unchanged: transactionSync already aborts on a throw (node_modules/lmdb/write.js:1024-1027); a test now pins it.

errorCases.scenario: A withWriteTxn callback throws after some writes.
errorCases.detection: The child transaction's callback throws; lmdb's batch runner catches it in the asChild branch and calls env.abortTxn() (node_modules/lmdb/write.js:663-680); the queued promise rejects with the stored error (:966-969).
errorCases.response: The child transaction's writes are discarded; withWriteTxn rejects with the callback's own error (confirmLockLoss still inspects it, as today).
errorCases.userImpact: The failed operation changes nothing in the store; the caller sees its error.

errorCases.detection: The step's child transaction callback throws inside runMigrations.
errorCases.response: The step's writes and its version write are aborted; the run rejects; earlier steps stay committed; the daemon's open fails as today and the next open retries the step.
errorCases.userImpact: The store is left at the last fully applied version, with no partial step.

errorCases.scenario: The store lost its locks while a write is queued.
errorCases.detection: The child transaction's promise does not settle; withWriteTxn's timer fires and probeForLockLoss reads the store (src/db/graph/store.ts:898-909).
errorCases.response: As today: recordLocksLost('a write transaction', 'write-timeout-probe', ...) and LmdbStoreLocksLostError.
errorCases.userImpact: As today: the daemon reports the lost locks instead of hanging.

errorCases.scenario: The store is ever opened in writemap mode.
errorCases.detection: lmdb's childTransaction throws 'Child transactions are not supported in writemap mode' (node_modules/lmdb/write.js:905-908).
errorCases.response: Every write fails loudly; a test pins the store's open options (no useWritemap) so this cannot change unnoticed.
errorCases.userImpact: Writes would fail immediately rather than silently lose atomicity.

edgeCases.input: Two callers' writes queued in the same lmdb batch, one throwing and one succeeding.
edgeCases.expected: The throwing caller's writes are discarded; the other caller's writes are committed (probed).
Its writes commit and its result is returned, exactly as before.

edgeCases.input: withWriteTxn called from inside another withWriteTxn callback.
edgeCases.expected: It is not a nested child: withWriteTxn first awaits getGraphStore(), so its child transaction runs after the outer callback's transaction (queued in a later batch); each commits or aborts on its own.

edgeCases.input: A callback that returns a Promise (async callback).
edgeCases.expected: Refused: the child transaction is aborted and the call rejects with 'withWriteTxn callbacks must be synchronous'; what the callback wrote before returning its Promise is not kept. The part after its first await still runs, detached, and any write it makes there is committed as its own write, so the compile-time type (no Promise-returning callback) is the guard; the runtime refusal only reports misuse.

edgeCases.input: An async migration step, while the store is opening.
edgeCases.expected: Runs as one child transaction with its version write; no other writer can reach the store until the open finishes, so nothing interleaves.

invariantsToPreserve.text: withWriteTxn's signature and its bounded wait and lost-lock reporting are unchanged (src/db/graph/store.ts:882-910).
Writes stay asynchronous and batched; no write path moves to a synchronous transaction.
After locks-lost no library transaction is called (store-health.test.ts:84-107), now including childTransaction.

migration.stateBefore: withWriteTxn (src/db/graph/store.ts:886), the migration runner (src/db/graph/migrations.ts:442-448) and the first-boot write (src/db/graph/store.ts:607-610) run their callbacks with lmdb-js root.transaction, which commits a callback's writes even when the callback throws (s1 bundle 2: node_modules/lmdb/write.js:655-704, probes). No stored data changes form.
migration.stateAfter: The three run their callbacks with root.childTransaction: a throwing callback's writes are aborted, other callers' batched writes commit, the async shape and the bounded lost-lock wait are unchanged. Tests pin the library behaviour.

migrationSteps.action: Switch the three call sites from root.transaction to root.childTransaction and correct the migration runner's comment; no stored data, schema version or key changes.
Add the regression tests (write-txn atomicity, migration step atomicity, library behaviour pin, store-health counting childTransaction, open options).
Update the installed daemon so the fix runs.

migration.backwardCompat: withWriteTxn's callback type is narrowed to synchronous callbacks (all 52 production callers already are; the one async test callback, src/db/graph/__tests__/store-health.test.ts:152, is rewritten to a synchronous one, with the library's childTransaction wrapped to resolve late so the bound is still exceeded); withWriteTxnSync, runMigrations and getGraphStore keep their signatures. The one behaviour change is the fix itself: a callback that throws no longer leaves its earlier writes behind. Four callbacks throw part-way today: upsertEntities (src/db/entities.ts:242, :254, UnregisteredRepoError for an unregistered repository part-way through a batch), reindexFile (src/db/entities.ts:410) and writeDocSummary (src/db/doc-summaries.ts:155); after the fix a batch that throws writes none of its entities instead of those before the bad one. That is the intended all-or-nothing outcome; the mixed-batch test src/db/__tests__/repo-strict-contract.test.ts:187-195 asserts only the registry and is unaffected. No store data is rewritten and SCHEMA_VERSION does not change.

alternativesConsidered.name: Run every store write callback as an lmdb child transaction
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: withWriteTxn, the migration runner and the first-boot write call root.childTransaction instead of root.transaction, so a throwing callback's writes are aborted while the batch, the async shape and the bounded lock-loss wait stay as they are.
alternativesConsidered.approach: withWriteTxn (src/db/graph/store.ts:882-910) accepts only a synchronous callback (its type no longer allows a Promise result, and a thenable result is refused by aborting the child transaction with a named error), because an async child callback holds lmdb's write transaction open across its await and a second caller arriving then would run nested inside it and lose its writes if the first throws (probed). It changes one call: `store.root.childTransaction(() => fn(store))` in place of `store.root.transaction(...)` at :886. Outside a write transaction lmdb queues it into the same shared batch as asChild (node_modules/lmdb/write.js:939), where the batch runner opens an abortable nested transaction and aborts it on a throw (:663-680); the promise still rejects with the caller's own error and still never settles on a store that lost its locks, so the race against the probe timer, confirmLockLoss and recordLocksLost are untouched. The migration runner (src/db/graph/migrations.ts:442-448), which keeps async steps because it runs inside the store's open before any caller can reach the store, and the first-boot write (src/db/graph/store.ts:607-610) make the same switch, so a throwing step leaves neither its rows nor the version write behind; the runner's comment is corrected. withWriteTxnSync already uses transactionSync, which aborts on a throw, and is unchanged. A regression test in the fresh-process harness pins the library behaviour (root.transaction keeps, childTransaction and transactionSync discard) so an lmdb upgrade that changes it fails a test.
pros: Fixes all 52 call sites through one line in the helper; no caller changes.
Keeps the async batching (no event-loop blocking), the bounded wait and lost-lock reporting exactly as they are.
Proven by probes: sync and async throwing callbacks leave nothing after a reopen, and their batch neighbours keep their writes.
cons: Relies on lmdb-js's child-transaction path, which is unavailable in writemap mode (the store does not use it; a test pins the open options).
A nested transaction per callback adds a small cost per write transaction.
withWriteTxn must refuse async callbacks (all 52 production callbacks are synchronous; one test's async callback is rewritten).

alternativesConsidered.name: Run every store write callback synchronously (transactionSync)
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: withWriteTxn wraps root.transactionSync in a promise, and the migration runner requires synchronous steps, so a throw aborts the whole transaction.
alternativesConsidered.approach: withWriteTxn calls `store.root.transactionSync(() => fn(store))` and returns its result as a resolved promise; the migration runner runs each step and its version write in one transactionSync, which requires every step's run to be synchronous; the first-boot write likewise. The bounded wait for a lost store is replaced by the synchronous path's handling (confirmLockLoss on the thrown error), since a synchronous call cannot be raced against a timer.
pros: transactionSync aborts on a throw (write.js:1024-1027), with no reliance on child transactions.
cons: Every write blocks the event loop for its whole duration and loses lmdb's batching of concurrent writes.
Removes the bounded wait that lock-loss-detection.test.ts proves: on a store that lost its locks a synchronous write may not return, and it cannot be raced against the probe timer.
Async migration steps (the runner's contract allows Promise<void>) would no longer be possible.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Atomic, but breaks the bounded lost-lock wait and blocks the event loop on every write.

alternativesConsidered.name: Keep root.transaction and undo a failed callback's writes
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: withWriteTxn records the keys a callback writes through a store proxy and, when the callback throws, writes their previous values back in the same batch.
alternativesConsidered.approach: withWriteTxn hands the callback a proxy GraphStore whose sub-DB handles record every put and remove with the key's previous value; on a throw it restores those values before rethrowing. The migration runner and first-boot write use the same proxy.
pros: Needs no change of lmdb transaction API.
cons: Every write path must go through the proxy; any direct handle use (for example root.openDB handles or dupsort getValues/remove pairs) escapes it.
Restoring is itself a set of writes that can fail, and dupsort values make 'previous value' ill-defined.
Much more code and risk than a one-line API switch, for a weaker guarantee.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Partial guarantees at the highest cost and risk.
